h: Treat the ring as flat and look for a mirror plane through the ring (perpendicular to it).
w: trans-1,2-Dimethylcyclohexane has chirality centers at C1 and C2 and no mirror plane, so it is chiral (it exists as the (1R,2R)/(1S,2S) pair). Ring flipping cannot remove chirality, because both chairs of one enantiomer are still that enantiomer.
x: cis-1,2-Dimethylcyclohexane has a mirror plane between C1 and C2 in the flat-ring view; it is meso.
trans-1,4-Dimethylcyclohexane has a mirror plane through C1 and C4 and no chirality centers; it is achiral.
cis-1,3-Dimethylcyclohexane has a mirror plane through C2 and C5; it is meso.

h: For the carbon bearing the methyl, are the two paths around the ring the same or different?
w: In 4-methylcyclohexanone the methyl carbon (C4) has two identical ring paths to the C=O, so it is not a chirality center, and a mirror plane passes through C1 and C4: achiral.
x: In 3-methylcyclohexanone the two ring paths from C3 differ (one reaches C=O after one carbon, the other after three), so C3 is a chirality center.
In 2-methylcyclohexanone C2 has C=O on one side and CH<sub>2</sub> on the other, so it is a chirality center.
In 3-methylcyclopentanone the two ring paths from C3 differ in length to the C=O, so C3 is a chirality center.

h: Find the chirality centers first (if any), then look for a mirror plane in the flat ring.
w: trans-1,3-Dimethylcyclopentane has chirality centers at C1 and C3 (each ring path differs in length to the other CH(CH3)). The only possible mirror plane, through C2 and the C4–C5 bond, would need both methyls on the same face. With one up and one down there is none: chiral.
x: cis-1,3-Dimethylcyclopentane has a mirror plane through C2 and the middle of the C4–C5 bond; it is meso.
cis-1,2-Dimethylcyclopentane has a mirror plane between C1 and C2; it is meso.
In trans-1,3-dimethylcyclobutane, C1 and C3 each have two identical ring paths, so there are no chirality centers, and a mirror plane contains both methyls: achiral.

q: Each chair conformation of cis-1,2-dichlorocyclohexane, taken alone, is chiral. Why is the compound nevertheless optically inactive and not resolvable at room temperature?
c: The ring flip converts one chair into its mirror image, and it is fast at room temperature
The axial C–Cl dipole cancels the equatorial C–Cl dipole
C1 and C2 are not chirality centers in the cis isomer
The two chairs have different energies, so only the achiral one is populated
h: Draw the chair with Cl axial at C1 and equatorial at C2, flip it, and compare the result with the mirror image of the starting chair.
w: In the cis isomer one Cl is axial and one equatorial. Flipping the ring swaps them, and the flipped chair is the mirror image of the first. Because the flip is fast at room temperature, the two enantiomeric chairs are always present 50:50 and cannot be separated: the compound behaves as the achiral (meso) cis isomer.
x: Dipole cancellation has nothing to do with optical activity, which depends on chirality, not polarity.
C1 and C2 each carry H, Cl, CHCl and CH<sub>2</sub>, so they are chirality centers; the cis compound is meso, not center-free.
Both chairs have one axial and one equatorial Cl, so they have equal energy; and neither single chair is achiral.

q: How many stereoisomers exist for 1,4-dimethylcyclohexane, and how many of them are chiral?
h: Are C1 and C4 chirality centers? Compare the two ring paths from C1.
w: The two ring paths from C1 (and from C4) are identical, so there are no chirality centers. The only stereoisomerism is cis/trans, and each has a mirror plane through C1 and C4. So there are 2 stereoisomers (cis and trans), neither chiral; they are diastereomers.
x: This counts the 1,2- or 1,3-isomer pattern (meso + a pair); 1,4-substitution has no chirality centers.
2<sup>2</sup> = 4 assumes two chirality centers, but C1 and C4 each have two identical ring paths.
There are two stereoisomers, but each has a mirror plane through C1 and C4, so neither is chiral.

q: A sample contains 80% of the (R) enantiomer and 20% of the (S) enantiomer. What is its enantiomeric excess?
w: ee = 80% − 20% = 60% in favor of R. Equivalently, 40% of the sample is racemic (20% R + 20% S) and 60% is excess R.
x: 80% is the fraction of R, not the excess of R over S.
40% is the racemic part of the sample (20% R + 20% S), not the excess.
The excess is in favor of the major enantiomer, R, and is 60%, not 20%.

q: A solution of 0.250 g of a pure chiral compound in 10.0 mL of ethanol gives an observed rotation of −1.30° in a 100-mm cell. What is the specific rotation?
h: [α] = α / (l × c), with l in decimeters and c in g/mL.
x: This uses l = 10 (centimeters); the path length must be in decimeters.
This uses c = 2.50 (g per 100 mL); the formula needs g/mL.
This uses l = 0.100 (meters); the path length must be in decimeters.

q: The pure (+) enantiomer of a compound has [α]<sub>D</sub> = +40.0. A synthetic sample has [α]<sub>D</sub> = +12.0. What percentage of the sample is the (+) enantiomer?
h: First find the optical purity (ee) from the rotations, then split the racemic remainder evenly.
x: 30% is the enantiomeric excess, not the percentage of the (+) enantiomer.
70% is the racemic portion of the sample.
35% is the percentage of the (−) enantiomer.

q: Pure (S)-X has [α]D = −24.0. A sample of X (0.300 g/mL, 0.500-dm cell) shows an observed rotation of +1.80°. What is the composition of the sample?
h: Convert the observed rotation to a specific rotation first. Then decide which enantiomer gives a positive sign.
w: [α] = +1.80 / (0.500 × 0.300) = +12.0. Since (S) is −24.0, (R) is +24.0, so a positive rotation means R is in excess. ee = 12.0 / 24.0 = 50% R. Composition: 50% + 25% = 75% R, 25% S.
x: The sign is positive, and (S) is levorotatory, so R must be the major enantiomer.
This divides by the concentration but not the path length (1.80 / 0.300 = 6.0, 25% ee); l = 0.500 dm must be included.
This both drops the path length and gives the excess to the wrong (levorotatory) enantiomer.

q: Pure (S)-Y has [α]D = +15.0. What observed rotation do you expect for a 90:10 mixture of (S)-Y and (R)-Y at 0.200 g/mL in a 2.00-dm cell?
h: Only the enantiomeric excess contributes to rotation. Find ee, then the sample specific rotation, then α = [α] × l × c.
w: ee = 90 − 10 = 80%, so the sample [α] = 0.80 × 15.0 = +12.0. α = 12.0 × 2.00 × 0.200 = +4.80°. The racemic 20% contributes nothing.
x: This uses 90% instead of the ee; the 10% R cancels an equal 10% of S.
This is the rotation of pure (S)-Y; the 10% R lowers it.
This leaves out the 2.00-dm path length.

q: A chemist mixes 3.0 g of the pure (R) enantiomer of a compound with 1.0 g of the racemate. What is the enantiomeric excess of the mixture?
h: Split the racemate into its R and S halves, then total R and S.
w: The racemate is 0.5 g R + 0.5 g S. Totals: R = 3.5 g, S = 0.5 g, out of 4.0 g. ee = (3.5 − 0.5)/4.0 = 75%. (Or: 3.0 g of the 4.0 g is unpaired R.)
x: 87.5% is the percentage of R (3.5/4.0), not the excess of R over S.
This treats the 1.0 g of racemate as if it were all S.
25% is the racemic fraction of the mixture (1.0/4.0).

q: An asymmetric reduction gives an alcohol in 90% ee. What is the ratio of the major to the minor enantiomer?
h: Convert ee to percentages: major = (100 + ee)/2.
x: 9:1 is 90:10, which is 80% ee.
10:1 is about 91:9, which is about 82% ee.
90:1 reads the ee as a percentage of one enantiomer and divides by 1; the minor enantiomer is 5%, not 1%.

q: Which property is different for the two enantiomers of 2-butanol?
c: The sign of the specific rotation
h: Enantiomers differ only in interactions with something chiral.
w: Enantiomers have identical physical properties in an achiral environment; they differ only toward chiral things, such as plane-polarized light. They rotate light by the same magnitude in opposite directions.
x: Boiling point depends on intermolecular forces, which are identical for mirror-image molecules.
Hexane is achiral, so both enantiomers dissolve in it equally.
IR absorptions depend on bond vibrations, which are identical in mirror-image molecules.

h: A sample rotates light only if it contains an excess of one enantiomer of a chiral compound.
w: The 70:30 mixture has a 40% excess of the (R) enantiomer, so it rotates light at 40% of the pure value: optically active.
x: A meso compound is achiral, so it does not rotate plane-polarized light.
A racemate has equal amounts of both enantiomers, whose rotations cancel.
cis-1,2-Dimethylcyclohexane is a meso compound (achiral), so it is optically inactive.

q: Racemic 2-phenylpropanoic acid is treated with one equivalent of enantiopure (S)-1-phenylethylamine. Which statement about the product is correct?
c: It is a mixture of two diastereomeric salts, which can be separated by crystallization
It is a mixture of two enantiomeric salts, which cannot be separated by crystallization
It is a single salt, because the (S)-amine reacts with only the (S)-acid
It is a racemic salt, which must be separated by chiral chromatography
h: Write the two salts as (R)-acid·(S)-amine and (S)-acid·(S)-amine. What is their relationship?
w: The amine deprotonates both acid enantiomers, giving (R)-acid·(S)-amine and (S)-acid·(S)-amine salts. These are not mirror images (the mirror of the first would be (S)-acid·(R)-amine), so they are diastereomers, with different solubilities that allow separation by fractional crystallization.
x: The two salts share the same (S)-amine, so they are not mirror images; enantiomeric salts would need the (R)-amine as well.
An acid–base reaction is not selective enough to leave one enantiomer untouched; with one equivalent, both acid enantiomers form salts.
Diastereomeric salts are separable by ordinary methods; chiral chromatography is not required.

q: Which reagent could be used to resolve racemic butan-2-amine, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Resolution of a base needs a partner that (1) forms a salt with an amine and (2) is a single enantiomer of a chiral compound.
w: (2R,3R)-Tartaric acid is an enantiopure chiral acid. With the racemic amine it forms two salts, (R)-amine·(R,R)-acid and (S)-amine·(R,R)-acid, which are diastereomers and can be separated by crystallization. Treating each salt with NaOH then frees the single amine enantiomer. The answer is (2R,3R)-tartaric acid.
x: meso-Tartaric acid is achiral, so its salts with the (R) and (S) amine are enantiomers and cannot be separated by crystallization.
1-Phenylethylamine is enantiopure but is a base; it does not form a salt with another amine. It is used to resolve racemic acids.
Acetic acid is achiral, so the two acetate salts are enantiomers with identical solubility.

q: In a classical resolution, 10.0 g of a racemic acid is converted to diastereomeric salts and separated, without recycling the unwanted enantiomer. What is the maximum mass of the pure (R)-acid that can be recovered?
h: How much of the racemate is the (R) enantiomer to begin with?
w: A racemate is 50% R. Resolution only separates what is present; it does not convert S into R. The maximum is 5.0 g (50% yield), and in practice less is recovered.
x: Getting 10.0 g of R would require converting the S enantiomer into R (racemizing and recycling it), which this process does not do.
2.5 g is half of the R that is present; a perfect separation recovers all 5.0 g.
7.5 g exceeds the 5.0 g of R that the racemate contains.

q: The less soluble salt, (R)-acid·(S)-amine, is collected from a resolution and shaken with aqueous HCl and ether. What is in the ether layer?
c: The (S)-acid, because protonation inverts the chirality center
The racemic acid, because the HCl racemizes it
h: Strong acid protonates the carboxylate. Which species stays neutral (ether-soluble), and which becomes a charged salt (water-soluble)?
w: HCl protonates the carboxylate, giving the neutral carboxylic acid, which moves into the ether. The amine becomes its water-soluble hydrochloride. No bond to the chirality center is made or broken, so the ether holds the (R)-acid, enantiomerically enriched; the (S)-amine can be recovered from the water with NaOH.
x: Proton transfer happens at the carboxylate oxygen, not at the chirality center, so the configuration is unchanged.
Racemization would require breaking a bond at the chirality center; a quick acid–base extraction does not.
In aqueous HCl the amine is protonated to an ammonium salt, which stays in the water layer.

q: Which compound contains chirality centers but is achiral?
h: You need a molecule with two or more chirality centers and an internal mirror plane.
w: cis-1,2-Dibromocyclopentane has two chirality centers (C1 and C2) and a mirror plane between them: it is a meso compound, achiral despite its chirality centers.
x: 3-Methylcyclopentene has one chirality center (C3) and no mirror plane, so it is chiral.
trans-1,2-Dimethylcyclopropane has two chirality centers but no mirror plane; it is chiral.
1,1-Dimethylcyclohexane is achiral, but it has no chirality centers (C1 carries two identical CH<sub>3</sub> groups).
